title: Frontend web development
description: How pages are built and shown in the browser.

lessons.title: How a browser shows a page

blocks.text: Every website goes through the same pipeline in the browser. The browser takes the files it downloaded and turns them into the pixels you see.

steps: Build the structure of the page

blocks.text: A project keeps these jobs in separate files. The structure, the look and the behavior can change independently.

blocks.code:
my-site/
├── index.html        structure
├── styles/
│   └── main.css      look
└── scripts/
    └── app.js        behavior

blocks.text: When a script changes the page, the browser runs the steps again for the part that changed. Keeping the work small is why pages feel fast.
A page is a tree. One root holds children, and each child can hold its own children. The nesting shows which parts belong together.

blocks.code:
page
├── header
│   ├── logo
│   └── navigation
│       ├── learn
│       └── duel
├── main
│   └── lesson
└── footer

blocks.text: Each element has a role. A navigation area holds links, and a heading names the section below it. Screen readers and search engines rely on these roles to understand the page.

rows: The user can act on it

blocks.text: Choose an element for its meaning first. How it looks comes later, in the styles.
Layout answers one question: where does each box go? Flexbox places children in a line and decides how the free space is shared between them.
Two ideas drive it. The direction says which way the children flow. The justify setting says what happens with the free space along that direction.

blocks.code:
row:     logo ........ links ........ button
column:  logo
         links
         button

blocks.text: Most layouts are a row inside a column, or a column inside a row. Nesting these two is enough for almost every screen.

title: Backend development
description: How servers receive requests and send back data.

blocks.text: A server is a program that waits for requests and answers them. The client, such as a browser or a phone, is the one that asks.
Each request stands on its own. The server knows who is asking only if the request says so, usually with a token that proves the login.

blocks.code:
api/
├── controllers/    receive requests, return responses
├── services/       the rules of the app
├── repositories/   talk to the database
└── models/         the shape of the data

blocks.text: Splitting the server into layers keeps each job in one place. A request passes through the layers in order, and each layer does only its own part.

lessons.title: Reading and writing with HTTP methods

blocks.text: A method tells the server what the client wants to do. The same address can accept different methods, and each one means something different.

blocks.code:
GET     /lessons/12    read lesson 12
DELETE  /lessons/12    remove lesson 12
POST    /lessons       create a new lesson

blocks.text: Repeating a GET changes nothing, so it is safe. Repeating a POST may create a second item. Knowing this helps when a request fails and has to be sent again.

title: Databases
description: How data is stored, found and kept consistent.

lessons.title: Why we store data in tables

blocks.text: Data has to outlive a single request. A database keeps it safely and lets many users read and write at the same time.
A row is one record, and a column is one property that every record has. Because each column holds one kind of value, the data stays predictable.
These four operations cover most of the work a database does. Learning to think in them makes every data feature easier to design.
Copying the same data into many places causes mistakes. A better way is to store each fact once and link to it by a key.
The primary key identifies one row. A foreign key stores the primary key of a row in another table, such as winner_id pointing at users.id.
If mara changes her name, every duel still points at the same row, so nothing has to be updated in two places. Database rules also stop a link from pointing at a row that does not exist.

title: Version control
description: How teams track and combine changes to code.

blocks.text: Version control records a project as a series of saved states. Each saved state is a commit, and the list of commits is the history of the project.

blocks.code:
commit 4f2a9c
author:   the person who made the change
date:     when it was saved
message:  why the change was made
changes:  which files and lines differ from before

blocks.text: Because every commit has a reason, the history explains the project later. A good message says why the change exists, not only what it touches.
A branch is a separate line of work. Commits on a branch do not touch the main line until you join them back.

steps: Commit the work on that branch
Merge the branch back into main

blocks.text: When two branches change the same lines, the merge cannot decide alone. That situation is a conflict, and a person decides which version to keep.
